beats.intro: Module three. [[sub]]Who issues bonds, who buys them, and how they are issued and traded.
beats.dims: Bond markets are organized along three dimensions. [[d1]]The issuer type, or sector. [[d2]]The credit quality. [[d3]]And the time to maturity. Sometimes also the geography, or sustainability. [[cmp]]And unlike stocks, an issuer rarely has just one instrument. A company may have one or two kinds of shares, but many debt instruments, in different maturities and currencies. One large technology company had more than eighty debt instruments, and one stock.
beats.ratings: Credit quality is measured by credit ratings. [[a]]They are letter grades, given by agencies such as Standard and Poor's and Moody's. [[b]]From triple A, the highest quality, down through double A, A, and triple B. [[ig]]Triple B minus, or Baa three, is the lowest investment grade. [[hy]]Below that is high yield, also called speculative grade, or junk. [[sov]]Developed market governments are usually the safest borrowers, often rated triple A. [[fa]]An investment-grade issuer that slips into high yield is called a fallen angel.
beats.issuers: Two corporate issuers show how this works. [[brwa]]BRWA is investment grade. It borrows unsecured, across the maturity range. Commercial paper for seasonal needs, medium-term notes, and long-term bonds for factories and equipment. Bank credit facilities back its short-term paper. [[vivu]]VIVU is high yield. It has fewer fixed assets, and less stable cash flows. So it relies on secured bank loans, a floating-rate term loan, and callable notes. It cannot use the commercial paper market. [[sov]]Governments sit at the safe end. Their right to tax gives them the lowest credit risk in their market.
beats.investors: Investors choose positions to match their needs. [[mm]]Short-term bond funds are liquid cash alternatives, so they hold short-term, high-quality bonds. [[core]]A core bond fund holds investment-grade bonds of medium and long maturity. [[pen]]Pension funds and insurers favor long maturities with fixed coupons, to match long-term liabilities. [[hy]]And investors seeking higher returns accept credit risk, often comparing high yield with equity. [[note]]A fund limited to investment grade could never buy VIVU's notes.
beats.indexdiff: Bond indexes work like stock indexes, with three differences. [[a]]First, one issuer can have many bonds, so bond indexes can have more than ten thousand constituents. [[b]]Second, bonds mature and new ones are issued, so there is much more turnover. Indexes are usually rebalanced monthly. [[c]]Third, bonds are weighted by the market value of debt outstanding, so governments, as large borrowers, often weigh heavily. [[d]]A fund that tracks an index usually holds a sample of the bonds, not all of them.
beats.indexes: Choose an index that matches the strategy. [[g]]A global aggregate index covers investment-grade, fixed-coupon bonds from all major issuer types, in many markets. It suits a core bond fund. [[e]]An emerging markets bond index covers dollar bonds of emerging market governments, a narrower, lower-credit universe. [[s]]A sustainable corporate index screens for credit quality and ESG criteria, and excludes issuers in some business lines. [[r]]A short-term investment-grade fund should be judged against an index of similar maturity and credit, not a broad one.
beats.primary: Now the primary market, where issuers sell new bonds. [[prim]]Primary markets raise capital. Secondary markets trade existing bonds between investors. [[debut]]A debut issuer, selling bonds for the first time, is often replacing a bank loan. [[pub]]A public offering is open to anyone. A private placement goes only to selected investors. [[rep]]Repeat issuers move much faster, and usually issue a new bond priced close to par.
beats.issuance: Investment-grade issuance can take just hours. [[t1]]The underwriters and issuer agree to launch, and the deal is announced. [[t2]]Investors hear from the issuer on a call. [[t3]]The deal launches with final size and pricing. [[t4]]It prices against a government benchmark. [[t5]]The final term sheet is delivered, and the bonds are free to trade. [[uw]]In an underwritten offering, the banks guarantee the sale at an agreed price. Frequent issuers use a shelf registration, to issue quickly. [[hy]]For lower credit quality, the banks may only try their best to sell the bonds, for a commission. [[sov]]Governments usually sell new debt by public auction.
beats.secondary: Secondary markets are mostly over the counter. [[otc]]Dealers quote prices, and investors trade with them, rather than on an exchange. [[spread]]The bid-offer spread, the gap between the price a dealer pays and the price it charges, measures liquidity. [[ladder]]Newly issued government bonds are the most liquid, with spreads of a fraction of a basis point. Recent bonds of frequent, high quality corporate issuers cost a few basis points. Older bonds of rare issuers, ten to twenty basis points or more. [[nt]]Some bonds hardly trade at all, so their prices are estimated from similar bonds.
beats.distressed: When an issuer nears bankruptcy, its bonds become distressed debt. [[a]]They trade far below par, because holders may not receive all the promised payments. In 2020, the bonds of one car rental company fell to under ten percent of par. [[b]]Investors limited to high ratings may be forced to sell. Hedge funds and other opportunistic investors often buy, seeking equity-like gains. [[c]]A year later the company reorganized, and the bonds recovered to their earlier price. [[d]]Unlike a stock, a bond keeps trading until the company liquidates or restructures.
beats.wrap: Let's recap. [[w1]]Bond markets are classified by issuer, credit quality and maturity. [[w2]]Investment grade is triple B minus and above. High yield is below. [[w3]]Bond indexes are broad, turn over fast, and weight by debt outstanding. [[w4]]New bonds sell in primary markets. Trading is mostly over the counter.
